title: The Dot and the Swarm
author: Ethan Mollick
summary: Ethan Mollick admits he got something large wrong: he expected humans to manage AI agents as a company manager would, with careful delegation and hand-built organization. He now sees that the Bitter Lesson applies to the org chart, because models themselves are getting good at organizing work, as with prompting and information retrieval before. He points to personal agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots, which learn context and act proactively, and to a swarm of thousands of agents that tackled a famous mathematics problem with only thin human coordination. He explains why self-organization works for agents, since much of human management exists to solve principal-agent problems, scattered information and expensive communication that agents mostly lack. He keeps caveats about long, unglamorous work and unexpected agent behavior, and ends with cautious optimism that cheap organizing could expand the work worth attempting, provided humans decide where to point the agents.
points: Mollick concedes that his earlier prediction, that managing agents would require careful human-designed structures, fell to the Bitter Lesson that brute-force capability beats elaborate human rules.
The test of a good agent is increasingly what you no longer have to tell it, since context is learned from your messages and plans are developed by the agent itself.
Large agent swarms coordinated themselves with a very thin human structure, which suggests organizing, not intelligence, was the part he overestimated.

Much of human management exists to manage human limits such as conflicting goals, hidden information and costly communication, so agents face fewer of those problems but still face principal-agent risks with their human owners.
If organizing becomes cheap, organizations can attempt more, and the human role shifts toward deciding where to point the agents and reassessing as work proceeds.
quotes: I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI.
It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do.
You don’t need to type in tons of context, the AI learns it from your messages. You don’t have to give them a plan, they develop plans themselves. They figure it out.

The company set the goals, but its coordination structure was remarkably thin: a few groups, one change of direction, and Codex passing the best ideas between them. Within each group, the agents transmitted ideas back and forth on their own.
This is the Bitter Lesson applied to the org chart. The organizational problem I thought would take years of careful human design was largely solved by models that are better at organizing.

People have their own goals, and those aren’t always the goals of organizations. We call this the principal-agent problem and a lot of the machinery of organizations, from bonuses to management structures, is based around solving it.
Agents have far fewer of these problems. They don’t angle for promotions or protect their turf. They don’t even have meetings.
When organizing is expensive, organizations only attempt what they can staff. When it gets cheap, the list of things worth attempting can grow.
